routes.title: Japan: bind procurement safety evidence to deployed model versions
routes.impactRationale: Editorial judgment, not measured risk reduction: the proposed addition ties existing supplier safety evidence to deployed versions, material-change retests and actionable incident duties. The platform's intended reach of approximately 180,000 officials indicates potential coverage, not purchasing power or vendor dependence. Public-sector scope, domestic-model emphasis and unverified executed lifecycle terms limit the claimed increment.
routes.feasibilityRationale: Editorial judgment: existing vendor benchmark/safety submissions, the procurement platform and AISI-assisted governance standard provide an administrative starting point. The rating remains conditional on a lawful future tender or agreed amendment. Final FY2027 terms, signatory delegation, budget authority, vendor capacity and enforceable remedies remain unverified. The May plan's November 2026–April 2027 targets do not prove present negotiability.
routes.actor: Japan's Digital Agency (builds and operates the whole-of-government platform Gen-nai, runs its rolling foundation-model procurements, published the Gen-nai Standard); ministry CAIOs administer agency-side use; AISI Japan as technical evaluator.
routes.obligor: Vendors of foundation models and AI systems bidding into Gen-nai and successor government AI contracts — under current calls principally developers of domestically built Japanese models; the standard's required appropriate selection of domestic and foreign foundation models keeps foreign models in scope for platform eligibility.
routes.instrument: Proposed lifecycle-evidence clauses in a lawful new Digital Agency tender and signed supply contract. The original vendor call already requires comparative benchmarks, safety explanations and partial-publication consent; the FY2027 plan adds tool-use, safety and supply-term submissions with separate paid procurement. Final tender terms, contracting delegation and amendment rights remain unverified.
routes.safeguard: Proposed incremental safeguard: bind evaluation evidence to the deployed model/tool version, retain reproducible deployment-level and stateful-agent tests, retest material changes, and specify incident deadlines, evidence preservation and proportionate cure/suspension where expressly contracted. Asking again for benchmarks or safety explanations repeats the existing vendor baseline; additional lifecycle duties and enforcement must be checked against executed terms.
routes.verification: The call already requires supplier evidence and partial-publication consent, and the FY2027 plan provides for Digital Agency evaluation after screening. Proposed addition: version-linked acceptance records, material-change retests and incident drills informing an authorised release decision. AISI participation, capacity, access and the operational gate delegation remain to be agreed; a shadow test alone does not prove contractual enforcement.
routes.remedy: Proposed: non-selection, suspension or termination where lawfully provided in the tender and signed contract, with notice and cure terms. Existing contract remedies were not reviewed; no AISI veto is established.
routes.window: The 2026-05-29 plan targets a November 2026 call, December close/screening, January 2027 evaluation/procurement notice, February results/bids, March award and April use. These changeable month-level targets are not confirmed day deadlines or evidence that terms are currently open. The original trial call closed in January 2026. Verify the new tender and authority before proposing additions; no unilateral rewrite of existing awards is assumed.
routes.evidenceSummary: Primary evidence reviewed 2026-10-31 corrects the earlier retrieval gap: the 2025-12-02 vendor call, Conditions bullets 2 and 7, already requires comparative benchmarks, explanations of hallucination/bias/harmful-content safeguards and consent to partial publication. The 2026-05-29 FY2027 plan, section 1 and section 2 items ④, ⑥, ⑨ and ⑩, provides for evaluation and tool-use, safety, supply-term and publication-consent submissions, with separate paid procurement. The Gen-nai Standard and Second AI Basic Plan document government governance and AISI technical support. Confidence remains Medium: supplier-facing baseline evidence is now documented, but additional version binding, retesting and actionable incident duties are proposals; final executed terms, signatory and enforcement remain unverified. Intended availability to approximately 180,000 officials is not measured use or bargaining power.
routes.gap: Executed FY2026 contracts, final FY2027 tender, existing version/change/incident duties, contracting and release-gate delegation, lawful amendment rights and remedies remain unverified. The guideline's own binding force and AISI operating role still need checking. Supplier willingness to accept additional lifecycle duties, testing costs, ministry budgets and quantified government AI spend are unknown.
routes.nextQuestion: Do executed terms and the final FY2027 tender already bind evidence to deployed versions, require material-change retests and define incident deadlines/remedies; if not, which authorised buyer and supplier can lawfully agree those additions before bids?
incentives: Vendors could gain access to a government platform intended for approximately 180,000 officials; spending and vendor dependence are not quantified.
The Digital Agency could make its existing supplier evidence actionable throughout deployment rather than repeat selection-stage safety explanations.
AISI Japan gains an operating channel for its evaluations, which the Second AI Basic Plan commits to wire into policy and operations.
Domestic-model demand may give suppliers a reason to accept bounded, priced lifecycle duties, but willingness, retest cost and substitute supply remain unverified.
constraints: The Gen-nai Standard assigns government-side duties, while the original call already imposes vendor-facing evidence conditions. Additional lifecycle obligations require a lawful instrument and supplier acceptance; their adoption is not established.

Current calls target domestically developed models, so the immediate obligor set is Japanese model developers; foreign labs are reached only through the standard's domestic-and-foreign model-selection duty.

The route rests on the government's own contracting authority; Japan's AI Act imposes no lab obligations and no penalties (team-verified read of the Cabinet Office overview), and competitive-procurement and budget rules still apply.
AISI Japan has no veto, and its evaluation-to-policy translation mechanism is a Basic Plan commitment, not an operating pipeline.

The call baseline is verified, but executed lifecycle and remedy terms are not. Version binding, retests and incident obligations count as additions only where not already required; published rollout targets do not establish drafting discretion.

sources.title: Digital Agency release: Gen-nai Standard published and AI-agent environments launched
sources.locator: Release paragraphs on the two agent environments, the standard's three roles, AISI cooperation, the model-case positioning and OSS Ver.2.0; attachment links to overview and full-standard PDFs.
sources.claim: Published 2026-10-20: the Digital Agency provides two AI-agent environments to ~180,000 government officials (agent chat from 2026-10-20; 源内工房 targeted ~Dec 2026); the Gen-nai Standard defines duties per role — users (officials), administrators, developers (Digital Agency staff) — and was drafted with the cooperation of AISI; it is offered as a model case for local governments and private businesses; Gen-nai OSS Ver.2.0, usable/modifiable/redistributable by anyone under a commercial-use licence, is slated for ~Feb 2027.

sources.title: Digital Agency: Government AI Gen-nai main policy page
sources.locator: Overview; 推進施策・取組内容 (3) 国内大規模言語モデル（LLM）開発支援; 展開スケジュール; press-release list (page last updated 2026-10-30).
sources.claim: All ~180,000 national officials are to use generative AI in FY2026; the Digital Agency frames procurement and use of domestically developed AI as promoting safe, secure AI use and Japan's AI autonomy (日本のAI自律性確保); rolling procurements are dated — domestic-LLM public call 2025-12-02 (results 2026-03-06), pre-announcement of a domestic foundation-model call 2026-05-29, trial of domestic foundation models on domestic cloud from 2026-07-10 — with full-scale use from FY2027 (Release 3.0) funded by participating ministries' budgets following spring-summer 2026 budget requests.

sources.title: Gen-nai Standard formulation/publication overview (Digital Agency PDF)
sources.locator: Slides: 源内基準の全体構造 1-2/1-3; 利用者（政府職員）が遵守すべき基本原則; 重層的なAIガバナンス体制の整備; quoted Second AI Basic Plan and Digital Priority Program excerpts. Full text extracted via download.
sources.claim: The standard's principles include establishing a foundation-model evaluation and selection system (基盤モデルの評価・選定体制の確立) and appropriate selection of domestic and foreign foundation models; user duties adopt a risk-based approach based on the AI Procurement and Utilization Guideline, with a high-risk determination sheet and CAIO reporting, human-in-the-loop (no direct copying of unverified AI output into official documents) and a shadow-AI ban; the governance diagram states the AI Act is the basis with basic plan, priority program and procurement guideline linked to cover policy through practice; the quoted Basic Plan excerpt commits the government to lead proper procurement and utilization so that AI used across Japanese society is reliable and transparent.

sources.title: Summary of Japan's Second AI Basic Plan (Cabinet Office PDF)
sources.locator: Strategic Pillar 3 (Lead AI Governance) key points; Four Principles; Strategic Pillar 1 reference on GENAI. Full text extracted via download.
sources.claim: Cabinet decision 2026-07-14: establish and enhance AISI's technical evaluation capabilities for AI model assessment, traceability, guardrails and crisis-time information sharing, while creating mechanisms to translate evaluation results into policy, regulatory and operational improvements; lead AI-governance development through the AISI International Network; convene an AI Summit in Japan at an early opportunity; update the Basic Plan annually and proactively review legal, regulatory and policy frameworks including the AI Act; advance Government AI through agentic AI and active use of Japan-developed models, supporting local-government adoption via GENAI open-sourcing.

routes.title: Compatible AI procurement safety profile across Japan, Korea and Singapore
routes.impactRationale: Editorial judgment, not measured risk reduction: one shared evidence bar would gate three public-sector markets at once, and mutual recognition would give vendors a single evaluation covering Japanese-, Korean- and regional-language failure modes that English-centric testing under-serves, while removing each government's incentive to undercut the others' safety asks as they compete for AI-leadership positioning. Bounded above by genuine cross-acceptance of substantive AISI evaluations becoming a regional default; bounded below by a paperwork harmonization that adds formats without new testing or reach beyond government sales.
routes.feasibilityRationale: Editorial judgment: joint AISI workshops and evaluation exercises offer a technical starting point. Governmental obstacles remain: this review did not locate mutual recognition of evaluation results for procurement, Singapore's whole-of-government procurement anchor, or authorization by the three governments for cross-acceptance. Different legal bases and multiple agencies add coordination costs. Technical cooperation does not establish procurement authority.
routes.actor: The three governments' AI-procurement and safety-institute authorities acting together: Japan's Digital Agency with AISI Japan; Korea's MSIT with its statutory AI Safety Institute (AI Basic Act Art. 12; the Public Procurement Service's role is unverified); Singapore's IMDA/GovTech with the Singapore AISI (Digital Trust Centre) — Singapore's whole-of-government AI procurement policy has not been located.
routes.obligor: Vendors of AI models and systems selling into the three governments' public-sector AI markets — foundation-model developers and integrators, and through them the labs whose models they deploy.
routes.instrument: Proposed common procurement clauses and an agreed evaluation-evidence recognition arrangement, adopted through each government's lawful procurement process. Technical guidance is a starting point, not contracting authority. Controlling procurement instruments in all three jurisdictions remain to be examined.
routes.safeguard: Proposed: a shared pre-deployment safety-evidence package covering Japanese-, Korean- and regional-language failure modes, accepted for covered purchases by all three governments, with compatible incident-reporting and model-change-notice clauses. No such recognition arrangement or common clause set was located in this review; absence from this evidence set does not establish absence across APAC.
routes.verification: Proposed: participating institutes evaluate against an agreed protocol, with procurement authorities accepting the results. Workshops and joint tests support technical feasibility, but neither evaluation equivalence nor procurement acceptance is established.
routes.remedy: Proposed: remedies expressly included in each jurisdiction's lawful tender and contract, potentially including non-selection or suspension. No common remedy, delisting power or executed clause set was located.
routes.window: No common procurement decision window was established. Published workshops and evaluation reports document cooperation, not government consent or open procurement negotiations. Retrieve current tenders and named decision-makers in each country.
routes.evidenceSummary: The reviewed primary sources document Japan-Korea AISI technical cooperation and Singapore's joint testing and evaluation activity. These provide a possible technical foundation for compatible evidence requirements, not an agreed purchasing arrangement. The shared procurement profile, recognition rules and government assent remain proposals. Korean statutory claims in the earlier working note were not re-verified against the amended controlling text and are not relied on here to establish procurement authority.
routes.gap: Singapore's whole-of-government AI procurement policy was not located. Korea's Public Procurement Service standards and amended AI Basic Act were not examined in this pass. Acceptance of foreign AISI evaluations for covered purchases is not established by these sources. Whether current tenders reference network evaluation formats is unknown. The operative procurement terms and government consent require direct verification.
routes.nextQuestion: Can the three institutes convert NAAIMES joint-testing methods into a shared evidence format that procurement officers accept — and does each government have a live procurement instrument to host it? First discriminating retrievals: Singapore's GovTech/IMDA procurement requirements, Korea's Public Procurement Service AI standards, and the Gen-nai call documents.
incentives: Vendors run one evaluation for three government markets instead of three duplicated ones, and gain a reason to test Japanese-, Korean- and regional-language failure modes that English-centric testing misses.
Governments could reduce duplicated testing and improve public-sector assurance if they agree on substantive evidence requirements.
A common evidence package could reduce vendor compliance work; savings and acceptance remain unmeasured.
The institutes gain uptake for methods they already co-produce — JAI-Trust, joint-testing formats, NAAIMES evaluator guidance.
Japan's planned AI Summit and Korea's APEC PPSTI chairmanship 2026-27 (team-verified) give each government a visible deliverable.
constraints: Mutual recognition for the proposed procurement route was not established by the sources reviewed.
Singapore's procurement-side anchor is missing: no whole-of-government AI procurement policy has been located in team research to date.

Three different legal bases — Korea's binding statute, Japan's guideline and contract machinery, Singapore's voluntary frameworks — must be bridged by a clause set rather than harmonized law, risking a lowest-common-denominator profile.
Multiple agencies per country must consent; there is no single contract hook comparable to Japan's Gen-nai platform.
Institute cooperation to date is technical and voluntary; nothing fetched shows any government has authorized cross-acceptance of evaluations for procurement.

sources.title: AISI Japan: Japan and Korea AISIs hold First Joint Technical Workshop
sources.locator: Overview and Day 2 sections (Japanese text with English translation below); published 2026-10-16 per URL slug and team-verified read.
sources.claim: Japan and Korea's AI Safety Institutes held their first joint technical workshop on 2026-10-08/09 with 30 researchers and engineers, aiming to lay the foundation for ongoing information sharing and collaboration; sessions covered evaluation methods that account for multilingual and multicultural factors, Japan's JAI-Trust generative-AI safety/security benchmark project, and Korea's multimodal red-teaming.

sources.title: Singapore AI Safety Institute: Resources page
sources.locator: Entries for the NAAIMES Best Practice Guidance Document (report, Jul 23, 2026), the SG-KR AISI joint evaluation of data-leakage risks in tool-using LLM agents (report, Jun 16, 2026), the 2026 Singapore Consensus and the 2026 Red Teaming Challenge report.
sources.claim: The AISI network, now styled the International Network for Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science (NAAIMES), released its first Best Practice Guidance Document on automated evaluation of large language models (Jul 2026) to support the third-party evaluator ecosystem; the Singapore and Korea AISIs jointly published an evaluation of data-leakage risks in tool-using LLM agents across 12 realistic tasks (Jun 2026), finding that task correctness alone is insufficient to assess agent safety; the page also lists the 2026 Singapore Consensus from the International Scientific Exchange and a 14-country red-teaming challenge.

sources.title: MSIT press release: Basic Act on AI passed at the National Assembly's plenary session
sources.locator: Third bullet (Safe and Trustworthy Foundation for High-Risk AI and Generative AI); first bullet (framework and AI Safety Institute); effective-date paragraph.
sources.claim: Korea's AI Basic Act (passed 2024-12-26, taking effect January 2026) establishes the AI Safety Institute as a specialized organization to protect citizens' lives, bodies and property from AI risks (Art. 12); imposes obligations ensuring transparency (Art. 31), safety (Art. 32) and operator responsibility (Art. 34) on high-risk and generative AI; and provides a legal basis for government support of voluntary private AI safety and trustworthiness verification and certification (Art. 30) and AI impact assessments (Art. 35).

sources.title: MDDI press release: Singapore announces new AI safety initiatives (AI Action Summit, Paris)
sources.claim: Singapore (11 Feb 2025): as co-lead of the AISI network's Testing and Evaluation Track, it released a Joint Testing Report with Japan assessing whether guardrails hold in non-English settings across 10 languages (including Japanese and Korean) and five harm categories; launched the Global AI Assurance Pilot (AI Verify Foundation + IMDA), a testbed convening testing vendors with deployers of real GenAI applications to shape assurance standards and grow the third-party assurance market; and published the Red Teaming Challenge Evaluation Report 2025, a consistent cross-language/culture methodology from 50+ participants across nine APAC countries.
